identification.summary: Iran-based group that MITRE says has been active since at least 2010 and moved from website defacement to malware-based cyber espionage by 2014, targeting the US defense industrial base and Iranian users of anti-censorship tools [S1]. FireEye's Operation Saffron Rose report described the group using fake conference lures, spoofed login pages and 'Stealer' malware that exfiltrated data over FTP [S4]. CrowdStrike tracks the same activity as FLYING KITTEN [S3]. MITRE also associates the Rocket Kitten / Operation Woolen-Goldfish reporting with this group as a potential relationship [S1].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 (defacement era) [S1]. CrowdStrike: tracking as FLYING KITTEN since mid-January 2014 [S3]. Rocket Kitten reporting: operating since at least mid-2014 [S8].
identification.notes: No Microsoft threat-actor name was found for this cluster in the sources gathered. MITRE G0130 groups Ajax Security Team, Flying Kitten, Operation Saffron Rose, AjaxTM, Operation Woolen-Goldfish and Rocket Kitten, but describes the Rocket Kitten link only as a 'potential relationship' based on infrastructure, tools and modes of operation [S1]. Ajax/Saffron Rose/Flying Kitten reporting comes from FireEye and CrowdStrike (2014) [S3]; Rocket Kitten, Woolen-Goldfish and Thamar Reservoir reporting comes from Trend Micro, ClearSky and Check Point (2015) [S5][S6][S8][S9]. Facts are kept attributed to the reporting vendor.

attribution.sponsor: Iran (suspected). FireEye assessed the Ajax Security Team was likely backed by the Iranian government but could not say whether it operated alone or within a larger coordinated effort [S4]. Press coverage of Check Point's Rocket Kitten report linked the group to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though Check Point's own wording was more cautious [S9].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only. FireEye: suspected Iranian-government backing; press coverage is inconsistent, with some quoting the report as calling the government relationship inconclusive [S4]. Trend Micro: Woolen-Goldfish 'possibly state-sponsored' [S5]. ClearSky: evidence points to Iranian hackers [S6]. Check Point: suggested an official body may have recruited local hackers; press coverage linked the group to the IRGC [S9]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Persian-language and Iran time-zone settings on most victim machines found on one C2 server [S4]; Iranian forum origins and defacement history [S1][S4]; Persian-language references in code (Rocket Kitten, per researchers Anderson and Guarnieri) [S10]; operational-security failures exposing a developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' [S9].

objectives: Espionage supporting Iranian state interests: collecting information from US defense contractors and monitoring Iranian dissidents and users of anti-censorship tools [S4]. Trend Micro and ClearSky judged Rocket Kitten was not after monetary gain but was keeping tabs on individuals affiliated with foreign-policy and defense actors [S8]. ClearSky assessed Thamar Reservoir access was sought for espionage or other nation-state interests [S6].

sectors: Diplomacy, defense and security, journalism, human rights [S6]
targeting.notes: FireEye identified 77 victims on one C2 server, most with Persian-language and Iran time-zone settings [S4]. ClearSky counted about 550 targets, mostly in the Middle East, in the Thamar Reservoir / Rocket Kitten activity [S6][S8]. Citizen Lab's 2015 diaspora 2FA-phishing report shares infrastructure and tactics with earlier Iranian campaigns but does not name this group [S7].

capabilities.summary: Low-to-moderate sophistication social engineering and credential theft. Spearphishing with fake conference (IEEE) lures and spoofed credential pages such as Outlook Web Access, followed by prompts to install a fake 'browser patch' [S3][S4]. Custom 'Stealer' malware exfiltrating data over FTP [S4]. Trojanized anti-censorship software [S4]. Rocket Kitten used GHOLE malware, a modified version of a Core Security penetration-testing tool, and later OneDrive links to files posing as PowerPoint presentations [S5]. Thamar Reservoir activity combined compromised trusted websites hosting fake pages, multi-stage malware, phone calls and social-media messages [S6]. Real-time phishing designed to defeat Gmail two-factor authentication was documented against Iranian diaspora targets (not attributed by name) [S7]. Telegram account takeover via intercepted SMS codes and abuse of Telegram's API to enumerate 15 million Iranian phone numbers was attributed to Rocket Kitten by outside researchers [S10]. ClearSky judged the operators technically unsophisticated and prone to mistakes [S6].

campaigns.name: Website defacements
campaigns.summary: MITRE says the group has been active since at least 2010, initially defacing websites before moving to espionage by 2014.

campaigns.name: FLYING KITTEN tracking begins
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike begins tracking FLYING KITTEN, observing targeting of multiple US defense contractors and political dissidents using spoofed login pages and 'Browser Patch' stealer downloads.

campaigns.name: Operation Saffron Rose
campaigns.summary: FireEye reports Ajax Security Team espionage against the US defense industrial base and Iranian anti-censorship tool users, with Stealer malware and 77 victims on one C2 server.

campaigns.name: Operation Woolen-Goldfish / GHOLE
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports Rocket Kitten spearphishing of Israeli and European organizations using GHOLE malware and OneDrive-hosted lures.

campaigns.name: Thamar Reservoir
campaigns.summary: ClearSky details an Iranian campaign against about 550 Middle East targets in diplomacy, defense, journalism and human rights, named after targeted Israeli researcher Thamar E. Gindin.

campaigns.name: Two-factor authentication phishing of Iranian diaspora
campaigns.summary: Citizen Lab documents phone-call-initiated real-time phishing to bypass Gmail 2FA; shares infrastructure with earlier Iranian campaigns but is not attributed by name.

campaigns.name: Rocket Kitten 2 (The Spy Kittens Are Back)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro and ClearSky report continued Rocket Kitten targeting of Israelis, Iranian exiles and opponents of Iran, focused on personal accounts.

campaigns.name: Rocket Kitten: A Campaign With 9 Lives
campaigns.summary: Check Point exposes main developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' after gaining access to a misconfigured group phishing server and a C2 server.

campaigns.name: Telegram account compromises
campaigns.summary: Researchers attribute compromise of more than a dozen Telegram accounts and enumeration of 15 million Iranian phone numbers to Rocket Kitten (reporting Reuters).

diamond.adversary: Iran-based operators who emerged from Iranian hacker forums and defacement activity; developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' exposed by Check Point [S1][S4][S9].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing, spoofed login pages, Stealer malware, GHOLE malware, trojanized anti-censorship tools, real-time 2FA phishing, SMS-code interception [S3][S4][S5][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Typosquat domains spoofing target organizations, FTP exfiltration servers, compromised trusted websites hosting fake pages, OneDrive-hosted lures [S3][S5][S6].
diamond.victim: US defense contractors; Iranian dissidents, activists and anti-censorship users; Israeli and European researchers, diplomats, journalists and defense personnel [S3][S5][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Monitoring of regime opponents and collection on foreign-policy and defense communities of interest to Iran [S4][S8].
diamond.technology: Webmail and OWA credential flows, SMS-based authentication, consumer messaging apps (Telegram) and personal accounts that bridge into corporate networks [S3][S8][S10].

gaps: Cluster boundary: MITRE treats Rocket Kitten as only a potential relationship to Ajax Security Team; FireEye/CrowdStrike (Ajax/Flying Kitten) and Trend Micro/ClearSky/Check Point (Rocket Kitten) reporting may describe distinct but related clusters [S1].
No Microsoft threat-actor name, and no US government attribution or indictment, was found for this cluster.

Primary documents not opened directly: FireEye Saffron Rose PDF, Check Point 'Campaign With 9 Lives' report, Trend Micro white papers, ClearSky Thamar Reservoir PDF and the MITRE G0130 page (WebFetch failed); details rely on search-result summaries and press coverage.
The FireEye PDF is labeled 2013 while coverage dates publication to May 2014; exact publication date unverified.
Citizen Lab's 2015 2FA phishing report does not attribute the activity to a named group; inclusion here reflects shared Iranian infrastructure only [S7].
Imported aliases Group 26, Sayad, Timberworm, TEMP.Beanie and Thamar Reservoir were not confirmed by a source gathered in this pass.
No reporting on activity after 2016 was found; current status (dissolved, renamed or absorbed into other Iranian clusters) is unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): key terrain is identity rather than networks: personal webmail, OWA portals, SMS-based 2FA and messaging accounts of defense staff, analysts and dissident contacts [S3][S7][S10]. STEP 2 (effects): personal-account compromise lets the actor bridge from weakly defended home networks into corporate accounts [S8]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): template is spoofed domain or lure (fake conference, OneDrive document), credential capture, then a stealer or GHOLE implant with FTP exfiltration [S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent credential phishing of defense-industry and policy personnel and their personal accounts for espionage [S3][S8]. MDCOA is real-time 2FA bypass or SMS interception against personnel with access to mission systems, enabling account takeover and contact-network mapping [S7][S10]. Candidate indicators: lookalike domains of the unit or contractor, unsolicited conference invitations, 'browser patch' download prompts after login, unexpected 2FA codes or calls from foreign numbers, outbound FTP from user endpoints [S3][S4][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse phishing reports from personal and official accounts, since this actor targets both [S8]. Authorities: personal and diaspora-contact accounts fall outside DODIN defensive authority; coordinate with counterintelligence and law enforcement. Mission assurance: phishing-resistant MFA instead of SMS codes and awareness training for staff targeted via conference and Iran-studies lures [S4][S7][S10]. Coordination: share lookalike-domain and C2 indicators with DIB partners, who were primary 2014 victims [S3].
